newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises to two-month high as mark sinks in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises to two-month high as mark sinks in Europe.

text.p: The dollar advanced to a two-month high against the mark Monday after the German currency came under attack in Europe and Germany's central bank president said major nations supported a higher dollar.

The dollar was carried up to 1.5010 marks, its highest level since July 16, as the mark also fell against the French franc and Italian lira amid speculation over Italy's reentry into Europe's exchange rate mechanism.
In late trading, the dollar was at 1.5003 marks, up from 1.4920 late Friday and 109.25 yen, little changed from 109.28 yen.
The dollar's gains were fanned after remarks by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who said the Group of 10 nations agreed on a desire for a strong dollar.
"We all agreed further dollar developement is important and a strong dollar is in the interest of all," Tietmeyer told reporters after a meeting of G10 central bank governors.
With the dollar passing the 1.4965 mark level, held since July, the market may start to bet on further gains above 1.50 marks, fuelling a scramble to buy dollars, dealers said.

"After the comments by Tietmeyer, it kind of paves the way a little bit," said Brian Arabia, assistant vice president at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago. "If the dollar goes up, it may have room to go further."

A weaker mark will make German exports more competitive in Europe and help bolster Germany's lackluster economy. Strong German economic growth is in turn desired by other European countries to spur domestic economic production.

"(The lira) has been helped by the debate ... in Europe over the central parity rate for the lira, when the Italian government decides to rejoin, which should be pretty soon," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
The Italian currency was forced out of the European Monetary System in September 1992 amid overwhelming speculation the lira would weaken against other currencies in Europe, particularly the mark.
Currently, currencies within the ERM are allowed to fluctuate by no more than 15 percent on either side of a fixed bilateral exchange rate against other member currencies.

The lira rose to a high near 1008 lira per mark from about 1015 lira earier in the day. The French and Germans seem to be stepping up pressure for a stronger lira central rate, probably 1000 against the mark, Gilmore said.

The French franc rebuffed recent gains by the mark after traders tired of speculating that the Sept. 18 release of France's 1997 budget would erode confidence in its ability to meet budget deficit targets for European currency convergence in 1999.
Dealers unwound bets on a weakening franc by selling the mark, which fell below 3.41 francs.

Last week, the Bank of France was reported to have intervened several times to defend the falling franc as the mark encroached on the psychologically important 3.43 French level. That was the bottom of the franc's old fluctuation band, before the ERM realignment in August 1993 widened bands from plus or minus 2.25 percent off central rates to 15 percent.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.2233 Swiss francs from 1.2189 on Friday and fell to Canadian $1.3704 from C$1.3728. The pound fell to $1.5568 from $1.5604 on Friday.
